Did we ever count our own 9/11s ?
results.description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, when “We Are All Americans” became a universal mantra, there is a pressing need to understand how the faces of terrorism and counter-terrorism have evolved globally. It is worth noting that Jammu and Kashmir experienced its own series of “9/11 moments” both before and after the 2001 attacks in New York. Yet, these repeated atrocities never invoked the same global reaction as the strikes on America. Now, as India takes decisive measures to defend its sovereignty by targeting terrorists and their backers directly across the border, the world is taking cues on how to fight terrorism: by taking the fight straight to the terrorists’ home. Had counter-terrorist operations been conducted with the speed and scale witnessed in recent years, the story of Jammu and Kashmir would have been different.The definition of a 9/11- style attackshould not be judged solely by the catastrophic event. Instead, the true gravity of terrorism needs to be analysed by the lethal intent of the perpetrators and their sponsors. It is precisely through this lens that Jammu and Kashmir reveals a long-standingsystemic pattern of such existential threats. Consequently, any discourse on global terrorism remains fundamentally incomplete without bringing Jammu and Kashmir into the frame. In the months following the 2001 attacks, the then-Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah, frequently shared a telling anecdote. His domestic help rushed into the living room, breathless, where Abdullah was seated with an American guest. The helper urged them to turn on the television, which was broadcasting live, horrific images of planes striking the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York. As the terror unfolded on screen, the American guest huddled in his armchair, paralyzed with fear, his face turning pale. The helper turned to Abdullah and asked in Kashmiri, “What has happened to the guest?” Abdullah replied: “They are witnessing terrorism for the first time—something we experience every single day. We kept telling them that terrorism hits us daily, but the Americans never paid attention. They could never truly understand the pain and horror we were going through. To this day, the deep pain of Kashmir remains misunderstood. Those who supported the Pakistan-sponsored terror project of “Azadi”—or in realistic terms, the violent separation of Kashmir from India—dismissed this suffering as a mere façade. A single brush painted the entire region. Observers failed to see the difference between actual terrorists, their support network, and ordinary citizens. Common people were caught in a violent crossfire, and that was never their choice. The September 11 attacks in America were viewed in stark black and white. The victims were not terrorist sympathizers, nor did an extensive local terror ecosystem exist there on the scale that took decades to build in Kashmir—a reality of bomb explosions, shootings, blood, and rows of lifeless bodies. Jammu and Kashmir witnessed this horrific scale of violence both before and after 9/11. We must understand where these tragedies and their true impact stand. Just weeks after the massive terror attack in America, terrorists targeted the J&K Assembly complex in Srinagar on October 1, 2001. Security forces foiled the takeover, but an explosive-laden vehicle and gunfire killed more than 30 people, including young college girls. This was a massive terror attack—truly the 9/11 of Kashmir. Yet unlike the aftermath in America, there was no global outrage and no talk of retaliation. That time L K Advani was Home Minister. America was busy with its planning to exact retribution from Al-Qaeda and Taliban, responsible for the terror attack with the active technical and material support from Pakistan’s ISI.The top leaders of the two – Osama bin Laden and Mullah Umar were found in Pakistan. Laden neutralized, and Mullah Umar died in a Karachi hospital. India witnessed yet another terror attack – December 13, 2001, when terrorists attempted to storm into theParliament in New Delhi. Amidst this upheaval, India witnessed yet another brazen assault on December 13, 2001, when terrorists attempted to storm the Parliament in New Delhi. The events of 9/11 fundamentally altered the landscape of global terrorism, and Kashmir was no exception. The Hurriyat leadership, which had previously shied away from condemning terrorism, abruptly awoke to this new global reality. Terrorism had finally assumed a definitive shape and narrative that was long overdue, driven by a shifted American attitude that fundamentally altered the discourse. Yet, there was a profound failure on the part of New Delhi’s central leadership, which seemed incapable of deciding on a clear policy to neutralize the threat. An all-out mobilization of troops to the borders yielded only a matching response from the Pakistani side, creating a volatile, war-at-any-moment scenario. Ultimately, it was the shuttle diplomacy of US and Western leaders that defused the situation. India’s so-called “coercive diplomacy” yielded nothing. By this time, a belief had entrenched itself in the Indian psyche—later reinforced by the 26/11 Mumbai attacks—that the country’s leadership lacked an effective counter-terrorism policy, or at least one that matched public expectations. While domestic terrorists were traced and neutralized, and top-notch measures were operationalized to curb infiltration across the Line of Control (LoC), a self-imposed red line remained: do not cross the border. The prevailing logic noted that while Sri Lanka and Pakistan routinely used aerial bombings on terror hideouts, India refrained from doing so. This thesis was premised on two flawed ideas: first, that India should avoid severe measures because a parallel attempt was underway to bring terrorists and their ecosystem to the negotiating table; and second, that India had to remain overly cautious about its international image, as if crossing borders were morally and politically corrosive. This was a misplaced and bizarre line of thought—driven by the fear that the world would be annoyed if Pakistan were hit for harbouring anti-India terrorists, and an inherent anxiety that domestic factions might rise against such actions. This passive approach was amplified not just once, but on several occasions. It raised a host of critical questions about whether Indian citizens were truly safe under a doctrine of self-restraint—a restraint that actively prevented actions that could have changed the course of counter-terrorism. At best, this was a hazy perception of our own making, a myth that desperately needed to be shattered. The Modi government changed the course. By launching the surgical strikes of September 2016 in retribution for the Uri attack; executing aerial strikes against a terror training Centre in Balakot, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, deep inside Pakistan to avenge the February 2019 Pulwama massacre; and finally executing Operation Sindoor in May 2025 to avenge the Pahalgam massacre, New Delhi arun has established an entirely new doctrine for responding to cross-border terrorism.

Minor reshuffle in Ladakh Police
results.description: In a key administrative reshuffle, The Ladakh Home Department has appointed 2015-batch Indian Police Service (IPS) officer Fulzele Piyush Nirakar as the new Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP), Leh. Nirakar, an IPS officer of the AGMUT cadre, succeeds outgoing SSP Shree Raam Raghavan, who has been transferred to the Cabinet Secretariat in New Delhi. Before his latest appointment, Nirakar served in Ladakh as SSP Security and SSP Telecommunications. Under the same administrative order, SSP Traffic Vikas Kumar has been assigned the additional charge of SSP Security and Police Telecommunication until further orders.
